Revised assessment incorporating literature:
The FOMC’s intermeeting 50 bp cut and accompanying liquidity operations are a textbook New Keynesian response to a negative shock. In policy-rule terms (Clarida, Galí, and Gertler), an adverse demand/supply disturbance from COVID-19 lowers expected output and inflation, warranting a preemptive easing of the policy rate. The commitment to “ample reserves” via T-bill purchases and continued repos is consistent with the post-2008 floor system that pays interest on reserves (introduced Oct. 2008) and with channel-system design discussed by Goodfriend (2002), aiming to prevent money market pressures from impairing policy transmission rather than to deliver outright QE. Lowering the primary credit rate aligns with modern applications of Bagehot’s lender-of-last-resort guidance—backstopping liquidity while maintaining a spread. The statement’s forward-looking language (“will act as appropriate”) reflects the recognized role of forward guidance in inflation-targeting frameworks (Svensson and Woodford, 2005). Given evidence on the credit channel (e.g., Gertler–Gilchrist) and term-structure transmission (Cochrane–Piazzesi), these steps help cushion financing conditions. Still, the explicit acknowledgment that “the coronavirus poses evolving risks to economic activity” tilts the tone modestly negative despite stabilization efforts.
